newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia debt battered,bills adjust for rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Australia debt battered,bills adjust for rate hike.

text.p: *The Australian debt market sold off sharply following a stronger than expected first quarter wages report, causing longer dated bill futures to adjust to a rate hike this year.
*U.S. April NAPM index due later on Thursday.

Australian debt sold off sharply following a stronger than expected first quarter wages report, which eroded hopes of any early easing in monetary policy and brought forward expectations of a tightening this year.
The benchmark November 2006 bond yield ended some 15 basis points higher than its initial U.S.-led lows on the data, and short-end yields spiked even higher.

June bill futures sank to indicate an unchanged policy by maturity, while further forward the December contract was close to fully pricing in a 50 basis points rate hike at 93.55, equating to a cash rate of 6.45 percent.
Next Tuesday's Reserve Bank board meeting is now expected to keep official interest rates at 6.0 percent, although prior to today's data they had been a slim chance of an easing.
Average weekly ordinary time earnings rose 1.3 percent to an annual growth rate of 4.6 percent, compared to a respective 0.8 and 4.3 percent forecast outcome.

"The latest wage figures will cause some discomfort at the Reserve Bank. Their former governor (Bernie Fraser) nominated 4.5 percent as the rate at which growth would fuel inflation and warrant a lift in interest rates," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank.
"(But) talk of rate hikes is absurd. The economy is moving forward but at a very modest pace," Kunnen added.

He, and other economists, are pointing to the stubbornly high unemployment rate at above 8.5 percent as a reason why the central bank will keep policy on hold, given that last year's three rate cuts were largely based on a weak labour market.
And Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia added: "Other than wages, all other factors are consistent with lower, rather than higher short term interest rates."
The focus locally now turns to Friday's March and March quarter retail trade data for an indication of consumer demand.

Local yield spreads blew out sharply against the dollar bloc on the wages data, particularly at the short end. U.S. debt had rallied on Wednesday, taking a stronger than expected GDP report in its stride and pinning hopes on a balanced budget agreement.
The U.S. April NAPM index is due later today.
